# Gel: Delegated Constraints, Multiple Inheritance, and a TypeScript Ingest Classifier

## Background
A hardware fleet team keeps its asset registry in a local **Gel 6** database (the graph-relational database formerly known as EdgeDB). Their compliance rules are expressed entirely as schema-level constraints, and a nightly batch job pushes a JSON manifest into the registry. Records that break a rule must not sink the whole batch: they have to be rejected individually, classified by the rule they broke, and reported.

Your job is to design the schema, migrate it, and build the batch ingest tool.

A local Gel 6 server is installed in this container but is not started automatically: run `bash /usr/local/bin/gel-ensure-server.sh` to bring it up (the helper is idempotent and blocks until the server accepts queries). Its connection settings are already supplied through preconfigured `GEL_*` environment variables — do not change them, and do not point the tool at any other instance. Everything else you need is already installed: the `gel` CLI, Node.js, TypeScript tooling and the `gel` npm client, with `node_modules` already populated. Treat the environment as offline and do not try to download packages.

## Requirements

### 1. Schema and migration
Design the schema for module `default` and apply it through Gel's migration system, so that `dbschema/migrations/` holds the applied migration(s) and the database reports being fully migrated.

The schema must contain exactly these object types, with exactly these pointer names:

- `Region` — required `key: str`. `key` must be unique across all `Region` objects; the violation must report the message `REGION_KEY_DUPLICATE`.
- abstract type `Revisioned` — required `revision: int64` whose minimum allowed value is `1`; the violation must report the message `REVISION_TOO_LOW`.
- abstract type `Taggable` — a **multi** property `tags: str`; every individual tag value must satisfy the shared token rule (below) with a length limit of `12`.
- abstract type `Asset`, which must extend **both** `Revisioned` and `Taggable`, with:
  - required `code: str` — must satisfy the shared token rule with a length limit of `16`, and must be unique **only among objects of the same concrete asset type**. The very same `code` value must remain insertable under a *different* concrete asset type. A same-type duplicate must report the message `CODE_DUPLICATE_IN_KIND`.
  - required `serial: str` — must be unique **across the whole `Asset` hierarchy**, i.e. a value used by one concrete asset type must be rejected for every other concrete asset type too. The violation must report the message `SERIAL_DUPLICATE_GLOBAL`.
  - required single link `region` pointing at `Region`.
  - required `slot: int64`, required `capacity: int64`, required `reserved: int64`.
  - the pair (`region`, `slot`) must be unique **only among objects of the same concrete asset type**; the same (`region`, `slot`) pair must remain insertable under a different concrete asset type. The violation must report the message `SLOT_DUPLICATE_IN_KIND`.
  - `reserved` must never be greater than `capacity`; the violation must report the message `CAPACITY_EXCEEDED`.
- `ServerAsset`, extending `Asset` — required `hostname: str`.
- `StorageAsset`, extending `Asset` — required `volume_gb: int64`.
- `Operator` — required `name: str`, unique across all `Operator` objects, violation message `OPERATOR_NAME_DUPLICATE`; plus a **multi** link `crew` pointing at `Asset` that carries a link property `role: str`. A single `Operator` must never be linked to two assets carrying the same `role` value (two *different* `Operator` objects may each use the same `role`). The violation must report the message `ROLE_DUPLICATE_FOR_OPERATOR`.

The **shared token rule** must be expressed as exactly one user-defined *abstract* constraint in module `default` that accepts a single `int64` parameter and is reused at both sites (`Asset.code` with `16`, `Taggable.tags` with `12`). No other user-defined abstract constraint may exist in module `default`. A value satisfies the rule when it matches the regular expression `^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*$` **and** its length is less than or equal to the parameter. A violation must report the message `TOKEN_INVALID(max=16)` for `code` and `TOKEN_INVALID(max=12)` for `tags`.

All of the messages above are the exact, complete error text the database must produce — no prefixes, no suffixes, no punctuation of your own.

### 2. Batch ingest CLI (TypeScript)
Build a re-runnable command-line tool that ingests a JSON manifest and writes a JSON report.

- It must read the manifest, make sure every region key it declares exists, then attempt every asset record against the live database, one record at a time, in strictly ascending `seq` order.
- A record that the database refuses must be recorded as rejected and must leave nothing behind in the database, while every following record is still attempted.
- Records are mapped to concrete types by their `kind` field: `"server"` -> `ServerAsset`, `"storage"` -> `StorageAsset`.
- The tool must be safe to run repeatedly against a database that already holds data: pre-existing rows must be honoured as uniqueness conflicts rather than crashing the run, and re-declaring already existing region keys must not fail.

## Implementation Hints
- Project path: `/home/user/assetreg`
- Command: `bash /home/user/assetreg/run-ingest.sh --input <manifest.json> --report <report.json>`. Both flags are mandatory and may appear in either order. Create `run-ingest.sh` yourself; it may launch whatever runtime you like as long as the TypeScript sources of the tool live under `/home/user/assetreg/src/` and drive the database through the `gel` npm client.
- Manifest format (UTF-8 JSON object):

  ```json
  {
    "regions": ["EU_WEST", "US_EAST"],
    "assets": [
      {
        "seq": 1,
        "kind": "server",
        "code": "ALPHA",
        "serial": "SN-0001",
        "region": "EU_WEST",
        "slot": 1,
        "capacity": 10,
        "reserved": 2,
        "revision": 1,
        "tags": ["WEB"],
        "hostname": "host-1"
      }
    ]
  }
  ```

  `seq` values are unique positive integers but are not necessarily contiguous or pre-sorted. The `assets` array may be empty. `tags` may be absent (treat as no tags). `hostname` and `volume_gb` may be absent; when a record omits the property its concrete type requires, the database itself must be the one to reject it. Every record in any manifest you will be given breaks at most one of the declared rules, and every `region` value used by an asset record also appears in `regions`.
- Report file: a JSON object whose top-level keys are exactly `total`, `inserted`, `rejected`, `results`, `reason_counts` and `schema`.
  - `total` is the number of asset records in the manifest; `inserted` and `rejected` are the counts of each outcome and must sum to `total`.
  - `results` is an array with one entry per asset record, ordered by ascending `seq`, each entry having exactly the keys `seq`, `kind`, `serial`, `status`, `reason`, `error_class`. `status` is `"inserted"` or `"rejected"`. For an inserted record `reason` and `error_class` are both `null`.
  - For a rejected record, `reason` is the constraint error message the database produced — that is, exactly the single-line message text declared for the violated constraint in your schema, with none of the extra diagnostic lines (query excerpt, `Details:`, `Hint:`) that the client appends to the raw error. When the database instead refused the record because a required value was absent, `reason` is the literal string `MISSING_REQUIRED`. `error_class` is `"ConstraintViolationError"` in the first case and `"MissingRequiredError"` in the second.
  - `reason_counts` maps every `reason` string that occurred at least once to how many times it occurred; reasons that never occurred must be absent.
  - `schema` is an object with exactly the keys `abstract_constraints`, `delegated_pointer_constraints` and `delegated_object_constraints`, and every one of its values must be derived from live schema introspection performed during the run — never from a hardcoded literal:
    - `abstract_constraints`: ascending array of the module-qualified names of all abstract constraints defined in module `default`.
    - `delegated_pointer_constraints`: ascending, de-duplicated array of `"<TypeName>.<pointerName>"` strings (type name written without its module prefix) for every constraint attached to a pointer of a module-`default` object type that is marked as delegated.
    - `delegated_object_constraints`: ascending, de-duplicated array of module-`default` object type names (without the module prefix) that carry at least one delegated object-level constraint.
- Exit codes: `0` when nothing was rejected, `2` when at least one record was rejected (the report file must still be written in full), and `1` when a required flag is missing or the manifest cannot be read or parsed (in that case no report file may be written and a diagnostic must go to stderr).
- The last line the tool writes to stdout must be exactly `SUMMARY inserted=<inserted> rejected=<rejected>` with the two integers from the report.

The official Node.js client library for Gel



Quickstart   •   Website   •   Docs   •   Discord   •   Twitter
This is the official [Gel](https://www.geldata.com) client library for JavaScript and TypeScript. If you're just getting started with Gel, we recommend going through the [Gel Quickstart](https://docs.geldata.com/learn/quickstart/overview/nextjs) first. This walks you through the process of installing Gel, creating a simple schema, and writing some simple queries. ### Requirements - Node.js 18+ - For TypeScript users: - TypeScript 4.4+ is required ## Basic usage > The examples below demonstrate only the most fundamental use cases for this > library. **[Go to the complete documentation site. >](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/clients/js#gel-js-intro)** ### Create a client A _client_ is an instance of the `Client` class, which maintains a pool of connections to your database and provides methods for executing queries. ```ts import * as gel from "gel"; const client = gel.createClient(); ``` ### Configuring the connection The call to `gel.createClient()` doesn't require arguments, as the library can determine how to connect to your database using the following mechanisms. 1. _For local development_: initialize a project with the `gel project init` command. As long as the file is within a project directory, `createClient` will be able to auto-discover the connection information of the project's associated instance. For more information on projects, follow the [Using projects](https://docs.geldata.com/learn/projects) guide. 2. _In production_: configure the connection using **environment variables**. (This can also be used during local development if you prefer.) The easiest way is to set the `GEL_DSN` variable; a DSN (also known as a "connection string") is a string of the form `gel://USERNAME:PASSWORD@HOSTNAME:PORT/DATABASE`. For advanced cases, see the [DSN specification](https://docs.geldata.com/database/reference/dsn) and [Reference > Connection Parameters](https://docs.geldata.com/database/reference/connection). ### Run a query ```ts import * as gel from "gel"; const client = gel.createClient(); await client.query("select 2 + 2"); // => [4] ``` Note that the result is an _array_. The `.query()` method always returns an array, regardless of the result cardinality of your query. If your query returns _zero or one elements_, use the `.querySingle()` method instead. If your query is guaranteed to return exactly one element, use the `.queryRequiredSingle()` method. ```ts // empty set, zero elements const q1 = await client.querySingle("select {}"); // ^? string | null // one element const q2 = await client.querySingle("select 2 + 2"); // ^? number | null // one element const q3 = await client.querySingle<{ title: string }>( // ^? { title: string } | null `select Movie { title } filter .id = '2eb3bc76-a014-45dc-af66-2e6e8cc23e7e';`, ); // exactly one element const q4 = await client.queryRequiredSingle("select 42;"); // ^? number ``` ## Generators Install the `@gel/generate` package as a dev dependency to take advantage of Gel's built-in code generators. ```bash npm install @gel/generate --save-dev ``` Then run a generator with the following command: ```bash $ npx @gel/generate [FLAGS] ``` The following ``s are currently supported: - `queries`: Generate typed functions from `*.edgeql` files - `interfaces`: Generate interfaces for your schema types - `edgeql-js`: Generate the query builder ### `queries` Run the following command to generate a source file for each `*.edgeql` system in your project. ```bash $ npx @gel/generate queries ``` Assume you have a file called `getUser.edgeql` in your project directory. ``` // getUser.edgeql select User { name, email } filter .email = $email; ``` This generator will generate a `getUser.query.ts` file alongside it that exports a function called `getUser`. ```ts import { createClient } from "gel"; import { getUser } from "./getUser.query"; const client = createClient(); const user = await getUser(client, { name: "Timmy" }); // ^? { name: string; email: string } ``` The first argument is a `Client`, the second is the set of _parameters_. Both the parameters and the returned value are fully typed. ### `edgeql-js` (query builder) The query builder lets you write queries in a code-first way. It automatically infers the return type of your queries. To generate the query builder, install the `gel` package, initialize a project (if you haven't already), then run the following command: ```bash $ npx @gel/generate edgeql-js ``` This will generate an EdgeQL query builder into the `./dbschema/edgeql-js` directory, as defined relative to your project root. For details on generating the query builder, refer to the [complete documentation](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/clients/js/querybuilder#generation). Below is a simple `select` query as an example. ```ts import { createClient } from "gel"; import e from "./dbschema/edgeql-js"; const client = createClient(); const query = e.select(e.Movie, (movie) => ({ id: true, title: true, actors: { name: true }, num_actors: e.count(movie.actors), filter_single: e.op(movie.title, "=", "Dune"), })); const result = await query.run(client); result.actors[0].name; // => Timothee Chalamet ``` For details on using the query builder, refer to the full [query builder docs](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/clients/js/querybuilder). ## Contribute Contributing to this library requires a local installation of Gel. Install Gel from [here](https://docs.geldata.com/learn/cli) or [build it from source](https://docs.geldata.com/resources/guides/contributing/code). ```bash $ git clone git@github.com:geldata/gel-js.git $ cd gel-js $ yarn # install dependencies $ yarn run build # build all packages $ yarn run test # run tests for all packages ``` > In order to be able to run all tests you need to have `gel-server` in your > path. This can be done by either running tests from within a Python 3.12 > virtual environment (you will have it if you built Gel locally), or by > [installing](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/cli/gel_server/gel_server_install) > specific Gel version and then adding its binary path to the `GEL_SERVER_BIN` environment variable. > Check [here](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/cli/gel_server/gel_server_info) > to find how to get the binary path. ## License `gel-js` is developed and distributed under the Apache 2.0 license.

Title: Constraints - Schema | Reference

URL Source: https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/constraints

Markdown Content:
Constraints give users fine-grained control to ensure data consistency. They can be defined on [properties](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/properties#ref-datamodel-props), [links](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/links#ref-datamodel-links), [object types](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/objects#ref-datamodel-object-types), and [custom scalars](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/links#ref-datamodel-links).

## Standard constraints

Gel includes a number of standard ready-to-use constraints:

[`exclusive`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::exclusive)Enforce uniqueness (disallow duplicate values)
[`expression`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::expression)Custom constraint expression (followed by keyword `on`)
[`one_of`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::one_of)A list of allowable values
[`max_value`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::max_value)Maximum value numerically/lexicographically
[`max_ex_value`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::max_ex_value)Maximum value numerically/lexicographically (exclusive range)
[`min_value`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::min_value)Minimum value numerically/lexicographically
[`min_ex_value`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::min_ex_value)Minimum value numerically/lexicographically (exclusive range)
[`max_len_value`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::max_len_value)Maximum length (`str` only)
[`min_len_value`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::min_len_value)Minimum length (`str` only)
[`regexp`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::regexp)Regex constraint (`str` only)

Example: enforce all `User` objects to have a unique `username` no longer than 25 characters:

Copy

type User { required username: str { constraint exclusive; constraint max_len_value(25); }; }

Constraints can be defined on object types. This is useful when the constraint logic must reference multiple links or properties.

Example: enforce that the magnitude of `ConstrainedVector` objects is no more than 5

Copy

type ConstrainedVector { required x: float64; required y: float64; constraint expression on ( (.x ^ 2 + .y ^ 2) ^ 0.5 <= 5 ); }

The `expression` constraint is used here to define custom constraint logic. Inside constraints, the keyword `__subject__` can be used to reference the _value_ being constrained.

Note that inside an object type declaration, you can omit `__subject__` and simply refer to properties with the [leading dot notation](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/computeds#ref-dot-notation) (e.g. `.property`).

Also note that the constraint expression are fairly restricted. Due to how constraints are implemented, you can only reference `single` (non-multi) properties and links defined on the object type:

Copy

type User { required username: str; multi friends: User; constraint expression on ('bob' in .friends.username); }

You can re-use constraints across multiple object types by declaring them as abstract constraints. Example:

Copy

abstract constraint min_value(min: anytype) { errmessage := 'Minimum allowed value for {__subject__} is {min}.'; using ( __subject__  >= min); } scalar type posint64 extending int64 { constraint min_value(0); } type User { required age: int16 { constraint min_value(12); }; }

Constraints can be defined on computed properties:

Copy

type User { required username: str; required clean_username := str_trim(str_lower(.username)); constraint exclusive on (.clean_username); }

Copy

Copy

You can also add constraints for [link properties](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/links#ref-datamodel-link-properties):

## Link's "@source" and "@target"

You can create a composite exclusive constraint on the object linking/linked _and_ a link property by using `@source` or `@target` respectively. Here's a schema for a library book management app that tracks books and who has checked them out:

Copy

type Book { required title: str; } type User { name: str; multi checked_out: Book { date: cal::local_date; constraint exclusive on ((@target, @date)); } }

Here, the constraint ensures that no book can be checked out to two `User`s on the same `@date`.

In this example demonstrating `@source`, we've created a schema to track player picks in a color-based memory game:

Copy

type Player { required name: str; multi picks: Color { order: int16; constraint exclusive on ((@source, @order)); } } type Color { required name: str; }

This constraint ensures that a single `Player` cannot pick two `Color`s at the same `@order`.

Custom scalar types can be constrained.

Copy

scalar type username extending str { constraint regexp(r'^[A-Za-z0-9_]{4,20}$'); }

Note: you can't use [`exclusive`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::exclusive) constraints on custom scalar types, as the concept of exclusivity is only defined in the context of a given object type.

Use [`expression`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::expression) constraints to declare custom constraints using arbitrary EdgeQL expressions. The example below uses the built-in [`str_trim()`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/string#function::std::str_trim) function.

Copy

scalar type title extending str { constraint expression on (  __subject__  = str_trim( __subject__ ) ); }

This section describes the syntax to declare constraints in your schema.

[{abstract | delegated}] constraint name [ ( [argspec] [, ...] ) ] [ on ( subject-expr ) ] [ except ( except-expr ) ] [ extending base [, ...] ]"{" [ using constr-expression ; ] [ errmessage := error-message ; ] [ annotation-declarations ] [ ... ]"}" ; where argspec is:[ argname: ] {argtype | argvalue}

This declaration defines a new constraint with the following options:

abstract
If specified, the constraint will be _abstract_.

delegated
If specified, the constraint is defined as _delegated_, which means that it will not be enforced on the type it's declared on, and the enforcement will be delegated to the subtypes of this type. This is particularly useful for [`exclusive`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/constraints#constraint::std::exclusive) constraints in abstract types. This is only valid for _concrete constraints_.

name
The name (optionally module-qualified) of the new constraint.

argspec
An optional list of constraint arguments.

For an _abstract constraint_ argname optionally specifies the argument name and argtype specifies the argument type.

For a _concrete constraint_ argname optionally specifies the argument name and argvalue specifies the argument value. The argument value specification must match the parameter declaration of the abstract constraint.

on ( subject-expr )
An optional expression defining the _subject_ of the constraint. If not specified, the subject is the value of the schema item on which the concrete constraint is defined.

The expression must refer to the original subject of the constraint as `__subject__`. The expression must be [Immutable](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/reference/edgeql/volatility#ref-reference-volatility), but may refer to `__subject__` and its properties and links.

Note also that `<subject-expr>` itself has to be parenthesized.

except ( exception-expr )
An optional expression defining a condition to create exceptions to the constraint. If `<exception-expr>` evaluates to `true`, the constraint is ignored for the current subject. If it evaluates to `false` or `{}`, the constraint applies normally.

`except` may only be declared on object constraints, and otherwise follows the same rules as `on`.

extending base[,...]
If specified, declares the _parent_ constraints for this abstract constraint.

The valid SDL sub-declarations are listed below:

using constr_expression
A boolean expression that returns `true` for valid data and `false` for invalid data. The expression may refer to the subject of the constraint as `__subject__`. This declaration is only valid for _abstract constraints_.

errmessage := error_message
An optional string literal defining the error message template that is raised when the constraint is violated. The template is a formatted string that may refer to constraint context variables in curly braces. The template may refer to the following:

*   `$argname` – the value of the specified constraint argument

*   `__subject__` – the value of the `title` annotation of the scalar type, property or link on which the constraint is defined.

If the content of curly braces does not match any variables, the curly braces are emitted as-is. They can also be escaped by using double curly braces.

annotation-declarations
Set constraint [annotation](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/annotations#ref-eql-sdl-annotations) to a given _value_.
